content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a guideline on complementary feeding for infants and young children aged 6–23 months. This guideline replaces previous recommendations for feeding breastfed and non-breastfed children in this age group. It was developed following rigorous procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development and provides evidence-based recommendations to support optimal nutrition during this critical developmental period. Complementary feeding refers to the introduction of foods in addition to breast milk or formula when these alone are no longer sufficient to meet a child’s nutritional needs. This process typically begins at 6 months of age and continues until 23 months, although breastfeeding may extend beyond this period. This stage is crucial for children to develop healthy eating habits, establish long-term dietary patterns, and reduce the risk of malnutrition, growth faltering, and nutrient deficiencies. Malnutrition during this time can lead to impaired growth, delayed motor and cognitive development, and increased risk of morbidity and mortality. In the long term, it may result in reduced work capacity, earning potential, and reproductive health, as well as an increased risk of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) such as obesity and type 2 diabetes. The guideline emphasizes the importance of continued breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond, as well as the introduction of complementary foods at 6 months of age. It highlights the need for dietary diversity, including daily consumption of animal-source foods (such as meat, fish, or eggs), fruits, and vegetables. Pulses, nuts, and seeds should also be included frequently, especially when other animal-source foods are limited. Starchy staple foods should be minimized due to their lower nutrient density and potential to include anti-nutrients that reduce nutrient absorption. The guideline advises against the consumption of unhealthy foods and beverages, such as those high in sugar, salt, and trans fats, as well as sugar-sweetened beverages and non-sugar sweeteners. It also recommends limiting the intake of 100% fruit juice. In contexts where nutrient requirements cannot be met through unfortified foods alone, the use of nutrient supplements or fortified food products, such as multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) or small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS), may be beneficial. However, these products should not replace a diverse diet and must be accompanied by messaging to reinforce optimal feeding practices. Responsive feeding practices are also encouraged, which involve allowing children to eat autonomously and in response to their physiological and developmental needs. This approach supports self-regulation in eating and promotes cognitive, emotional, and social development. The guideline acknowledges gaps in evidence for many of the recommendations and calls for further research, particularly randomized controlled trials, to strengthen the evidence base. It also highlights the need for broad policy actions to support implementation, such as agricultural policies, front-of-package labeling, and marketing regulations. The recommendations are intended for a wide audience, including policymakers, technical staff, and program implementers in government institutions, non-governmental organizations, and other relevant sectors. The guideline aims to support global efforts to reduce stunting, wasting, and childhood overweight, as well as to achieve several targets within the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
